property_summary: For any deployed C instance, owner() returns the address stored in the first immutable arg slot (the owner slot); the mutant makes owner() return the collateral immutable slot instead, so there exist input immutable args where owner() != collateral(), breaking the rule.

For any immutable constructor args passed to the clone, owner() returns the address encoded in the first immutable slot (offset 0x0); the mutant returns the address at offset 0x14 (collateral slot), so for some input tuples owner() != collateral() and the mutant will differ.

For any deployed C instance, owner() returns the immutable address stored in the owner slot (immutable arg at offset 0x0); the mutant returns the immutable at offset 0x14 (collateral slot), so there exist immutable-argument inputs where owner() != collateral() and thus owner() would differ between reference and mutant.

For any deployed C clone with its immutable args, the owner() return equals the address encoded at immutable offset 0x0; the mutant returns the address at 0x14 (collateral slot) so when those two immutable addresses differ the mutant's owner() value differs — test fuzzes two addresses to find such a case.

For any two addresses encoded as immutables for owner (slot 0x0) and collateral (slot 0x14), the reference contract's owner() always returns the immutable at slot 0x0; the mutant returns the immutable at slot 0x14 so when the two immutables differ the mutant's owner() differs — fuzz two addresses and assert owner() equals the first (owner) immutable.

For any deployed C, collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable offset 0x14; the mutant returns the address at 0x28 instead and thus will differ for some immutable calldata, so there exists inputs where collateral() differs between reference and mutant.

For any immutable constructor calldata, C.collateral() always returns the address encoded at offset 0x14 (so the returned ERC20 address equals address(uint160(_getArgAddress(0x14)))) while the mutant returning from 0x28 will differ for some calldata; thus referencing the stored collateral slot offset 0x14 is invariant and the mutant breaks that for some inputs.

For every deployed C instance, collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant instead reads offset 0x28 and thus for some immutable constructor calldata the returned address differs, violating this rule.

For any deployed reference C, collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant reads offset 0x28 instead, so there exist immutable calldata where collateral() returns a different address — the test asserts that calling collateral() does NOT revert and returns an address equal to the address read at offset 0x14 from c's immutables (i.e. the contract's collateral getter is consistent).

For any deployed reference C, calling collateral() always successfully returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant reads offset 0x28 instead, so there exist immutable calldata for which collateral() still returns successfully but with a different address, violating this invariant.

For any input, C.debt() returns the ERC20 wrapping exactly the immutable address stored at offset 0x28 (no arithmetic); the mutant that adds 1 to the address will sometimes produce a different returned address and thus violate this equality.

For every call, C.debt() returns an ERC20 whose address equals the stored immutable address (no arithmetic); the mutant that adds 1 to the stored address will make the returned address differ for some inputs.

For any stored immutable address at offset 0x28, C.debt() returns an ERC20 whose address equals that stored address; the mutant returns an ERC20 whose address equals the stored address plus 1 (as uint160), so for some stored addresses the returned ERC20 address differs and the property is violated.

For any immutable arguments packed into the clone, the reference C.debt() returns an ERC20 whose address exactly equals the stored immutable address at offset 0x28; the mutant returns address(uint160(stored)+1) so for some stored addresses the returned ERC20 address will differ, violating equality.

For any 20-byte address A encoded as the immutable debt argument in the clone, calling C.debt() (which returns an ERC20) yields an ERC20 whose address equals A; the mutant adds 1 to the stored address (as uint160) so for some encoded addresses the returned ERC20.address differs (e.g. when A != A+1), which the test will detect by constructing a clone with a fuzzed immutable debt address and asserting equality between the stored immutable arg read via the clone's debt() and the expected original address.

For every call, C.debt() returns the immutable-deployed ERC20 address embedded in the clone (non-zero for valid deployment); the mutant returns address(0) breaking that rule for some inputs where the embedded immutable arg is non-zero.

For any clone instance c, calling c.debt() returns the ERC20 address embedded as an immutable constructor argument (i.e. not the zero address when the embedded arg is non-zero); the mutant returns address(0) (cast to ERC20) breaking this for clones whose embedded debt arg is non-zero.

For any deployed C clone, calling debt() returns the ERC20 address embedded as the immutable argument (i.e. not the zero address when the embedded immutable arg is non-zero); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this invariance for clones whose embedded debt arg is non-zero.

For any deployed C clone whose immutable 'debt' arg is nonzero, calling debt() returns a nonzero ERC20 address (reference satisfies this for all inputs); the mutant always returns address(0) (so for clones with a nonzero embedded debt arg the property is violated).

For any clone C deployed via CoolerFactory with a nonzero immutable 'debt' arg, calling c.debt() returns a nonzero ERC20 address (reference satisfies this for all inputs); the mutant returns address(0) breaking the property for some inputs (clones whose embedded debt arg is nonzero).

For any deployed C, the owner() address (immutable arg at offset 0x0) is not equal to the returned debt() address (immutable arg at offset 0x28) — the reference returns the debt arg, while the mutant incorrectly returns the owner arg cast as the debt token, making owner()==debt() for inputs where they differ; the correct contract therefore always returns the true debt immutable, and the mutant can produce equality with owner() for some inputs, violating that rule.

For every immutable args blob the reference contract returns debt() equal to the immutable arg at offset 0x28 (the configured debt token); the mutant instead returns the owner arg at offset 0x0 cast as the debt, so there exist inputs where debt() equals owner() in the mutant but not in the reference.

For every deployed C instance, debt() returns the immutable argument stored at offset 0x28; the mutant incorrectly returns the owner immutable (offset 0x0) cast as the debt, so there exist inputs where debt() == owner() in the mutant but debt() != owner() always holds for the correct contract.

For any deployed C instance, debt() must not equal owner() (the debt immutable is at offset 0x28 while owner is at 0x0); the mutant returns the owner address cast as the debt token for some deployments, making debt()==owner() and breaking the rule.

For every deployed C instance, debt() returns the immutable argument placed at offset 0x28 (the configured debt token); the mutant returns the owner immutable (offset 0x0) cast as the debt, so there exist deployments where debt() != owner() and the mutant makes them equal, violating this property.

For any deployed C, debt() returns the ERC20 address passed as the immutable argument at offset 0x28 (the declared debt token); the mutant returns the collateral arg at 0x14 instead and thus for some inputs debt() will differ from the true immutable debt address.

For any calldata used to construct C via its constructor clone data, the reference contract's debt() returns the immutable arg at offset 0x28 (the declared debt token), whereas the mutant returns the address from offset 0x14 (collateral) — thus the property: debt() != collateral() for at least some admissible inputs (i.e., when the two immutable addresses differ), which the mutant breaks by returning collateral instead of the true debt address.

For any deployed C clone, the debt() getter always returns the immutable debt address passed at offset 0x28 (and thus is equal to address(uint160(uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(address_at_offset_0x28))))?) — concretely: for any two distinct addresses a_collateral and a_debt, the reference satisfies debt() != collateral(), while the mutant that returns the collateral address as debt() will make debt() == collateral() for those inputs, so there exist inputs where the property fails.

For any deployed C clone, the reference always returns debt() equal to the immutable argument located at offset 0x28 and thus debt() != collateral() whenever the two provided immutable addresses differ; the mutant returns the collateral arg (offset 0x14) as debt(), making debt() == collateral() for inputs where the original had distinct addresses, so there exist fuzzed inputs (distinct collateral and debt addresses) that make the mutant violate debt() != collateral().

For any deployed C clone, the debt() getter always returns the immutable debt address passed at offset 0x28; the mutant returns the collateral address (offset 0x14) instead, so there exist inputs where debt() != collateral() (reference holds for all inputs) but the mutant yields debt() == collateral() for those inputs, violating the rule.

For every input, the reference contract's debt() returns exactly the immutable argument address packed at offset 0x28 (no bit-mangling); the mutant clears the low bit of that address so for some immutable arg values the returned address differs.

For any supplied immutable args blob, the reference C.debt() returns exactly the embedded address at offset 0x28; the mutant clears the low bit of that embedded address before returning, so for some fuzzed immutable-address values the returned address differs (i.e. reference returns an address whose low bit can be 1 while mutant always returns low bit 0).

For any immutable args embedded in the clone, C.debt() returns the exact address stored at offset 0x28 (including its low bit); the mutant clears that low bit so for some immutable addresses (those with low bit = 1) the mutant returns a different address.

For any arbitrary 160-bit address value encoded as the immutable arg at offset 0x28, the reference C.debt() returns that exact address (including its least-significant bit); the mutant clears the low bit before returning, so for some fuzzed immutable-address inputs whose LSB = 1 the mutant's return differs and the property is violated.

For any 160-bit address value provided as the immutable arg at offset 0x28, the reference C.debt() returns that exact address (including its least-significant bit); the mutant clears the least-significant bit before returning, so when the embedded address has LSB = 1 the mutant's return differs and the property is violated.

For any deployed C the factory() getter returns the address stored at immutable arg offset 0x3c (the factory address) — the mutant that reads offset 0x28 will sometimes return a different address (the debt address) for some immutable args, so calling factory() can return a different value under that mutant.

For any deployed C clone initialized with encoded immutables (owner, collateral, debt, factory), calling factory() returns the factory immutable; the mutant reading a different immutable offset can return the debt address instead, so factory() must equal the factory immutable value extracted from the same calldata encoding used to create the clone.

For any clone instance created with immutables encoded as (owner, collateral, debt, factory), calling factory() returns the factory immutable; the mutant that reads a different offset will sometimes return the debt immutable instead, so factory() must equal the factory field encoded into the clone and the mutant will violate this for some inputs.
